\chapter{Greetings}
\label{ch:greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in German, recognize the reply, and choose an appropriate response.}

The German greetings, built from their pieces — a word for \textquotedblleft{}good,\textquotedblright{} the day-parts, and the three-gender article system. Because German and English are siblings, most words here are direct cousins, reshaped by the High German Consonant Shift; where it helps, Spanish and French stand alongside for contrast. Writing begins with the same familiar cousin: follow one visible Hallo, then copy it once while the model stays in sight — no hidden spelling and no second word are due. GE-C01-practice closes the chapter by running the whole arc, casual to bedtime.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hallo]{hallo — \textquotedblleft{}hello,\textquotedblright{} and this time it \emph{is} a cousin}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-hallo}



\begin{quote}
Your first German word — and a reassuring one, because German and English are close cousins: \emph{both are Germanic languages}. That kinship will help you all through this book, and \emph{hallo} is the first proof.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item German \textbf{h} is pronounced (not silent like Spanish/French): \emph{HA-lo}.
  \item German \textbf{a} is a clean, open \emph{ah}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hallo} — informal \textquotedblleft{}hello / hi.\textquotedblright{} Unlike Spanish \emph{hola} (which only \emph{looks} like \textquotedblleft{}hello\textquotedblright{} by coincidence — a false friend), German \textbf{hallo} and English \textbf{hello} are the real thing: both grew from the same old Germanic hailing call (\emph{hala}, a shout to get attention or hail a ferryman), the same family as English \emph{holla}, \emph{hollo}, and \emph{hail}. Nineteenth-century English \textquotedblleft{}hello\textquotedblright{} was even shaped partly by German \emph{hallo}.

\begin{quote}
The pattern to carry through this whole book: because English is a Germanic language, German words are often \textbf{direct cousins} of English words — same family, no Latin middleman. (The Romance languages like Spanish and French reach English mostly \emph{through} Latin; German reaches it directly.)
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\emph{hallo} is informal-to-neutral — fine among friends, and increasingly common generally. Polite or first meetings often use a daytime greeting instead. You will build that greeting one familiar piece at a time over the next few lessons.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Writing — follow one word you can see}
Keep \textbf{Hallo} visible. Trace directly over it, then copy it once in large, slow letters. Say \emph{HA-lo} while your hand moves. Stop there.

This is not spelling from memory and not free writing. Your eye and hand are only following a word whose meaning and sound are already on the page.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hallo\textquotedblright{} — \emph{HA-lo}, with a real \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hallo\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}hail\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}holler\textquotedblright{} — the true hailing family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is German \emph{hallo} a real cousin of English \emph{hello}, or a coincidence like Spanish \emph{hola}? (A real cousin — same Germanic hailing root.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Hallo]{Hallo — copy one greeting with help}

\label{lesson:GE-W01-hallo-guided-copy}



\begin{quote}
Point to \textbf{Hallo} and say it once: \emph{HA-lo}. The model stays on the page.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — one guided copy}
Copy \textbf{Hallo} once on the line below it. Begin with the tall capital \textbf{H}, then follow with \textbf{allo}. Look back at the model whenever you want.

Say the word as you finish. Then draw one small line under the \textbf{H} that German and English inherited in the same old hailing family.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Compare your copy with the model. If one letter differs, repair only that letter. No hiding, no spelling test, and no second word today.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gut]{gut — \textquotedblleft{}good,\textquotedblright{} and the sound-law that reshapes German}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-gut}



\begin{quote}
This word starts most German greetings. It's a direct twin of English \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} — and the \emph{tiny} difference between them (\emph{good} vs \emph{gut}) opens the single most useful decoding rule in the language.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item German \textbf{u} = \emph{oo} as in \emph{food} or English \emph{boot}: \emph{goot}. The final \textbf{t} stays crisp — never softened. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gut} — \textquotedblleft{}good.\textquotedblright{} Root: Proto-Germanic \textbf{*gōdaz} — and English \textbf{good} comes from the \emph{exact same} word. No Latin in sight; German and English just inherited it from their shared Germanic parent.

So why \emph{gut} and not \emph{good}? One sound-law:

\textbf{The High German Consonant Shift.} Long ago, German (but not English) pushed a whole set of consonants forward. One of its rules: \textbf{d $\to$ t}. So every English \emph{d} tends to show up as \emph{t} in German:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{German} \\
\midrule
goo\textbf{d} & gu\textbf{t} \\
\textbf{d}ay & \textbf{T}ag \\
be\textbf{d} & Be\textbf{tt} \\
\textbf{d}o & \textbf{t}un \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

It's a single regular sound-law — the same kind of trick that reshaped the Romance languages (Latin \emph{-ct-} became Spanish \emph{-ch-}, \emph{noche}). Learn the shift once, and you can guess the English cousin behind a German word (and vice-versa) on sight. More rules of the shift as we go.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: German merges \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{}}]
English splits \emph{good} (adjective) from \emph{well} (adverb); Spanish splits \emph{bueno} from \emph{bien}; French splits \emph{bon} from \emph{bien}. \textbf{German does not} — \emph{gut} is \emph{both}. \textquotedblleft{}A good day\textquotedblright{} is \emph{ein guter Tag}; \textquotedblleft{}I'm doing well\textquotedblright{} is \emph{mir geht's gut}. One word covers the whole job. So the Romance \emph{bien/bueno} pair collapses back into a single German word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gut\textquotedblright{} — \emph{goot}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gut\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} — the d$\to$t shift
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tag\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}gut\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} — same shift, twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
English \emph{d} becomes which letter in German? (\emph{t} — \emph{good$\to$gut}, \emph{day$\to$Tag}.) Does German split \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} like English? (No — \emph{gut} is both.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der / die / das]{der, die, das — \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} and the gender English \emph{and} the Romance languages lost}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-der-die-das}



\begin{quote}
Before your first noun: German's words for \textquotedblleft{}the.\textquotedblright{} Many European languages tag every noun with a grammatical \emph{gender} — Spanish and French each run two — and German has it too, but with a twist neither of them kept.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{der} = \emph{dair}, \textbf{die} = \emph{dee}, \textbf{das} = \emph{dahss}. The \textbf{r} of \emph{der} is barely a vowel-like murmur at the back of the mouth, not an English \emph{r}; \emph{die} rhymes with English \emph{see}; the final \textbf{s} of \emph{das} is a sharp \emph{ss}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{der} — \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} (masculine). \textbf{die} — \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} (feminine). \textbf{das} — \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} (neuter). Roots: the old Germanic demonstratives \textbf{*sa / *sō / *þat} (\textquotedblleft{}that one\textquotedblright{}) — the \emph{same} family as English \textbf{the} and \textbf{that}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{das} $\leftrightarrow$ English \textbf{that} (the High German shift again: English \emph{t} $\to$ German \emph{s}, so \emph{that $\to$ das}).
  \item \textbf{die} $\leftrightarrow$ the \emph{-y} of English \textbf{the}/\textbf{they}.
\end{itemize}

Unlike Spanish \emph{el/la} and French \emph{le/la} (both from Latin \emph{ille/illa}), German's articles are cousins of English's own \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} — Germanic all the way.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: German kept THREE genders}]
Here's the twist. Latin had three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter); Spanish and French \textbf{collapsed to two}, folding neuter into masculine. German \textbf{kept all three}: \emph{der} (masc.), \emph{die} (fem.), \emph{das} (neut.). So a German noun is one of \emph{three} classes, not two — and, as everywhere, the gender is unpredictable and must be learned \emph{with} the noun and its article. English, meanwhile, threw gender out entirely and kept a single \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} — the opposite extreme. Your next nouns will let you practise that pairing.

One more thing coming later: German articles also change by \textbf{case} (their job in the sentence), so \emph{der} has other forms (\emph{den, dem, des}). Ignore that for now; just learn \emph{der / die / das} as the three \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}s.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}die\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}das\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}das\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{} — the t$\to$s shift
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der\textquotedblright{} for masculine, \textquotedblleft{}die\textquotedblright{} for feminine, \textquotedblleft{}das\textquotedblright{} for neuter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many genders does German keep, vs Spanish/French? (Three vs two — German kept the neuter, \emph{das}.) What English word is \emph{das} a cousin of? (\emph{That}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Tag]{Tag — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} a straight cousin of English \emph{day}}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-tag}



\begin{quote}
Your first German noun. In Spanish \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} was \emph{día} (via Latin); in French, \emph{jour} (via a longer Latin detour). In German it's \emph{Tag} — and it's simply English \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} with one consonant shifted.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item der / die / das — gender; \emph{Tag} is masculine, \emph{der Tag}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Tag} = \emph{tahk} — a long open \emph{a}, the vowel of English \emph{father}; Germans harden a final \emph{-g} to a \emph{k} (\textbf{final devoicing}), so \emph{Tag} rhymes with English \emph{tock}, not with English \emph{tag}. German nouns are always \textbf{Capitalized} (every noun, not just names).
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{der Tag} — \textquotedblleft{}the day\textquotedblright{} (masculine). Root: Proto-Germanic \textbf{*dagaz} — and English \textbf{day} is the same word. The only difference is the High German Consonant Shift from the \emph{gut} lesson (\textbf{d $\to$ t}): \emph{dagaz} $\to$ English \emph{day}, German \emph{Tag}.

So the three Romance-and-Germanic \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} words line up by ancestry:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Spanish \emph{día}, French \emph{jour} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{dies} / \emph{diurnum}
  \item German \textbf{Tag} $\leftrightarrow$ English \textbf{day} $\leftarrow$ Germanic \emph{*dagaz}
\end{itemize}

Two entirely different roots for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} (Latin \emph{dies} vs Germanic \emph{dagaz}) — which is why \emph{día} and \emph{Tag} look nothing alike, even though both languages are cousins far enough back.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens}]
\emph{Tag} is \textbf{masculine} (\emph{der Tag}) — learn it with its article, as always. Also note the capital \emph{T}: German writes \textbf{every} noun with a capital letter, a spelling rule no other language here shares.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Tag\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dair tahk}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tag\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} — hear the d$\to$t shift
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Tag} and English \emph{day} share a Germanic root; the shift is which consonant change? (\emph{d$\to$t}.) What's odd about how German writes \emph{Tag}? (Capitalized — all German nouns are.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Guten Tag]{Guten Tag — assembled, and a first taste of German endings}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-guten-tag}



\begin{quote}
Snap \emph{gut} and \emph{Tag} together for the standard polite greeting. But notice — \emph{gut} shows up as \emph{gut\textbf{en}}, and that extra \emph{-en} is your first glimpse of how German adjectives work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item gut · Tag
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Guten Tag} = \textbf{gut} (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{Tag} (\textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}good day,\textquotedblright{} the neutral polite \textquotedblleft{}hello\textquotedblright{} for daytime. Said \emph{GOO-ten tahk}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why \emph{guten}, not \emph{gut}?}]
Like every Germanic and Romance adjective, German \emph{gut} \textbf{agrees} with its noun — but German adjectives agree in \emph{more} dimensions than Spanish or French: not just gender and number, but \textbf{case} (the noun's job in the sentence). \emph{Guten Tag} is a frozen piece of a fuller phrase: \emph{ich wünsche Ihnen einen guten Tag}, \textquotedblleft{}I wish you a good day.\textquotedblright{} In that fuller thought, \textquotedblleft{}a good day\textquotedblright{} is the \emph{object} of the wish (the accusative case). For a masculine noun in that role, \emph{gut} takes the ending \textbf{-en}: \emph{guten}.

Don't try to master German's ending system now — it's a later chapter. Just bank two things: (1) German adjectives take endings that shift with gender, number, \emph{and} case; (2) the greeting is really \textquotedblleft{}(I wish you a) good day,\textquotedblright{} which is why it's \emph{guten}. A later bedtime greeting will give you a gentle contrast with a feminine noun and a different ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Guten Tag\textquotedblright{} — \emph{GOO-ten tahk}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Hallo\textquotedblright{} (casual) then \textquotedblleft{}Guten Tag\textquotedblright{} (polite) — the register gap
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Guten Tag} literally shortens from what fuller phrase? (\textquotedblleft{}{[}I wish you a{]} good day.\textquotedblright{}) Why the \emph{-en} on \emph{gut}? (Adjective agreement — masculine, accusative.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Morgen]{Morgen — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} hiding in your English \emph{tomorrow}}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-morgen}



\begin{quote}
The morning word — and a straight English cousin again, once you spot it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Tag — same build ahead: \emph{guten} + this noun.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Morgen} = \emph{MOR-gun} — stress the first syllable; the \emph{g} is a hard \emph{g}; the German \emph{r} is soft and guttural; the unstressed \emph{-en} sinks to a soft \emph{-un}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{der Morgen} — \textquotedblleft{}the morning\textquotedblright{} (masculine). Root: Proto-Germanic \textbf{*murganaz} — the same root as English \textbf{morning}, \textbf{morn}, and the \emph{-morrow} in \textbf{tomorrow} (\textquotedblleft{}to-morrow\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}at {[}the{]} morning {[}to come{]}\textquotedblright{}). No Latin detour; German \emph{Morgen} and English \emph{morning} are the same Germanic word, barely changed.

\begin{quote}
A small false-friend warning for later: German \emph{Morgen} can also mean \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}} A later farewell will reuse it with that meaning. Context tells the two senses apart; English keeps them in separate words (\emph{morning} vs \emph{tomorrow}), while German lets \emph{Morgen} do both jobs.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens}]
\emph{Morgen} is \textbf{masculine} (\emph{der Morgen}) — so, like \emph{Tag}, it will take \emph{guten} in the greeting.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Morgen\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dair MOR-gen}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Morgen\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — the same root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What English words share \emph{Morgen}'s root? (\emph{morning}, \emph{morn}, \emph{to-morrow}.) \emph{Morgen} is masculine — so \textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{} will use \emph{gut} with which ending? (\emph{guten} — like \emph{guten Tag}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Guten Morgen]{Guten Morgen — good morning}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-guten-morgen}



\begin{quote}
Same assembly as \emph{Guten Tag}, one noun swapped. Nearly free.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Guten Tag · Morgen
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Guten Morgen} = \textbf{gut} (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{Morgen} (\textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}good morning.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Morgen} is masculine, exactly like \emph{Tag}, so \emph{gut} takes the same \textbf{-en}: \emph{guten} — no new agreement to learn. Said \emph{GOO-ten MOR-gen}.

Used in the morning (roughly until midday); after that, German switches to \emph{Guten Tag}. You will build the evening greeting next, from the same familiar pattern.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Guten Morgen\textquotedblright{} — \emph{GOO-ten MOR-gen}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Guten Morgen\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Guten Tag\textquotedblright{} — morning, then midday
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is it \emph{guten} Morgen (same ending as \emph{Guten Tag})? (\emph{Morgen} is masculine too.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Abend]{Abend — \textquotedblleft{}evening,\textquotedblright{} cousin of English \emph{eve}}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-abend}



\begin{quote}
The evening word — a quieter English cousin than the others, but a real one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Tag — the same \emph{guten} + noun build.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Abend} = \emph{AH-bent} — stress the first syllable; a long open \emph{a}; the final \emph{d} hardens to a \emph{t} sound (German de-voices final consonants, exactly as it did to the \emph{-g} of \emph{Tag}).
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{der Abend} — \textquotedblleft{}the evening\textquotedblright{} (masculine). Root: Proto-Germanic \textbf{*ābanþs} — the same root as English \textbf{eve} and \textbf{even(ing)} (as in \emph{Christmas Eve}, \textquotedblleft{}the eve of…\textquotedblright{}). English wore it down to \emph{eve}; German kept more of it as \emph{Abend}. Same Germanic word for \textquotedblleft{}the close of the day.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{quote}
Contrast worth banking across all four languages: \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{} has a \emph{different} root in each branch — Germanic \emph{ābanþs} (German \emph{Abend}, English \emph{eve}), vs Latin \emph{sērus} \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{} (French \emph{soir}) and Latin \emph{tardus} \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{} (Spanish \emph{tarde}). The Romance pair named it after \emph{lateness}; the Germanic pair named it after the \emph{evening-down} of the day.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens}]
\emph{Abend} is \textbf{masculine} (\emph{der Abend}) — so, again, \emph{guten} in the greeting. Three masculine day-parts in a row (\emph{Tag}, \emph{Morgen}, \emph{Abend}) all take \emph{guten}. The next day-part is feminine, so it will gently show you a different ending without adding a new rule to memorize now.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Abend\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dair AH-bent}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Abend\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}eve\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Abend} is a cousin of which English words? (\emph{eve}, \emph{evening}.) Is it masculine or feminine? (Masculine — \emph{der Abend}, takes \emph{guten}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Guten Abend]{Guten Abend — good evening}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-guten-abend}



\begin{quote}
The evening member of the set. Same \emph{guten}, one more masculine noun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Guten Tag · Abend
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Guten Abend} = \textbf{gut} + \textbf{Abend} (masculine) = \textquotedblleft{}good evening,\textquotedblright{} \emph{GOO-ten AH-bent}. \emph{guten} again — the third masculine day-part in a row.

You now have the daytime arc: \textbf{Guten Morgen} (morning) $\to$ \textbf{Guten Tag} (midday/afternoon) $\to$ \textbf{Guten Abend} (evening). All \emph{guten}, all masculine. Only bedtime is left — and it breaks the pattern.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Guten Abend\textquotedblright{} — \emph{GOO-ten AH-bent}
  \item the arc — \textquotedblleft{}Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All three day-greetings use \emph{guten} — because their nouns are all which gender? (Masculine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Nacht]{Nacht — \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} where all four of your languages meet}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-nacht}



\begin{quote}
This is the best cross-language word in the whole chapter. German \emph{Nacht}, English \emph{night}, Spanish \emph{noche}, French \emph{nuit} — \textbf{all four are the same word}, traced back far enough. Here's the family reunion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item der / die / das — \emph{Nacht} is feminine, \emph{die Nacht}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Nacht} = \emph{nahkht} — the \textbf{ch} is the guttural \emph{loch} sound: a scrape at the back of the mouth, after the open \emph{a}, and \textbf{not} an English \emph{ch}. It is the same throat-scrape as Spanish \emph{j} (\emph{jamón}) and Arabic \emph{kh}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{die Nacht} — \textquotedblleft{}the night\textquotedblright{} (feminine). Root: it goes all the way back to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European *nók\textsuperscript{w}ts} (\textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}) — the deep ancestor of \emph{every} one of your night-words:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Branch} & \textbf{Word} \\
\midrule
German (Germanic) & \textbf{Nacht} \\
English (Germanic) & \textbf{night} \\
Spanish (Latin) & \textbf{noche} \\
French (Latin) & \textbf{nuit} \\
(the Latin itself) & \emph{noctem} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

They split apart by each branch's own sound-laws — Germanic turned the \emph{kt} into \emph{ht} (\textbf{Nacht}, \textbf{night}; that's Grimm's Law), while Latin kept \emph{ct} (\emph{noctem}), which Spanish then softened to \emph{-ch-} (\textbf{noche}) and French to \emph{-it-} (\textbf{nuit}). Four languages, four rules, one PIE word. When you say \emph{Nacht}, you're saying the same ancient syllable as \emph{noche} and \emph{nuit}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens}]
\emph{Nacht} is \textbf{feminine} — \emph{die Nacht} — inherited from its Germanic gender (and it matches feminine \emph{noche/nuit/noctem}, all feminine too). Its gender matters immediately: it's why \textquotedblleft{}good night\textquotedblright{} is \emph{gut\textbf{e} Nacht}, not \emph{guten}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Nacht\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dee nahkht}, guttural \emph{ch}
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}Nacht, night, noche, nuit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Nacht, night, noche, nuit} all descend from one PIE word — roughly what? (\emph{*nók\textsuperscript{w}ts}, \textquotedblleft{}night.\textquotedblright{}) Is \emph{Nacht} masculine or feminine? (Feminine — \emph{die Nacht}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Gute Nacht]{Gute Nacht — good night, and the ending that finally changes}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-gute-nacht}



\begin{quote}
The greeting that breaks the \emph{guten} streak — and shows you exactly what German's endings are tracking.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item gut · Nacht
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Gute Nacht} = \textbf{gut} (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{Nacht} (\textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}good night,\textquotedblright{} \emph{GOO-te nahkht}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \emph{gute}, not \emph{guten}}]
Three greetings in a row were \emph{gut\textbf{en}} (Tag, Morgen, Abend — all masculine). This one is \emph{gut\textbf{e}}. The reason is the one you set up: \emph{Nacht} is \textbf{feminine}, and a feminine noun in the \textquotedblleft{}(I wish you a) good \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} accusative takes the ending \textbf{-e}, not \textbf{-en}. So the endings line up:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gut\textbf{en} Tag} / \emph{Morgen} / \emph{Abend} — masculine $\to$ \textbf{-en}
  \item \emph{gut\textbf{e} Nacht} — feminine $\to$ \textbf{-e}
\end{itemize}

That single vowel is German's adjective quietly reporting the noun's gender — exactly the job \emph{bueno/buena} and \emph{bon/bonne} did in Spanish and French, just with German's own endings.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Like Spanish \emph{buenas noches} and French \emph{bonne nuit}, \emph{Gute Nacht} is the \textbf{bedtime} farewell — \textquotedblleft{}sleep well,\textquotedblright{} said on parting for the night, not an evening hello (that's \emph{Guten Abend}). Same split French makes; German keeps the greeting (\emph{Abend}) and the send-off (\emph{Nacht}) apart.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Gute Nacht\textquotedblright{} — \emph{GOO-te nahkht}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Guten Tag\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Gute Nacht\textquotedblright{} — hear \emph{-en} vs \emph{-e}, and say why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why \emph{gute} Nacht but \emph{guten} Tag? (\emph{Nacht} is feminine, \emph{Tag} masculine — the ending agrees.) Is \emph{Gute Nacht} a greeting or a bedtime farewell? (Bedtime farewell.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die (plural)]{die — one article for every plural}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-die-plural}



\begin{quote}
You have learned three words for \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} one per gender. Here is the relief: in the plural there is only ever \textbf{one}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \emph{die} for every plural}
\begin{quote}
Singular: \textbf{der} Tag · \textbf{der} Morgen · \textbf{der} Abend · \textbf{die} Nacht Plural: \textbf{die} Tage · \textbf{die} Morgen · \textbf{die} Abende · \textbf{die} Nächte
\end{quote}

Whatever the noun's gender, the plural article is \textbf{die}. \emph{der} $\to$ \emph{die}, \emph{das} $\to$ \emph{die}, \emph{die} $\to$ \emph{die}. Three genders in the singular collapse to one form in the plural — German, like French with \emph{les}, spends a single article on every plural noun there is.

\begin{sounds}
Many German plurals bend the vowel as well as adding an ending. \emph{Nacht} $\to$ \emph{Nächte}: the open \emph{a} of \emph{nahkht} is fronted to \textbf{ä}, the vowel of English \emph{bed}, so \emph{Nächte} is \emph{NEKH-tuh}. That two-dot mark is called an \textbf{umlaut}, and the vowel change it writes down is one of German's regular plural signals.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four day-parts in the plural}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} & \textbf{what changed} \\
\midrule
der Tag & \textbf{die Tage} & article, plus \emph{-e} \\
der Morgen & \textbf{die Morgen} & article only — the noun is unchanged \\
der Abend & \textbf{die Abende} & article, plus \emph{-e} \\
die Nacht & \textbf{die Nächte} & article, plus \emph{-e}, plus the umlaut \emph{a $\to$ ä} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

German plurals are not built from one rule the way English adds \emph{-s}. Each noun carries its own plural, which is why a German noun is worth learning as a set of three: \emph{der Tag, die Tage}. The one thing that never varies is the article.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Tag, die Tage\textquotedblright{} — singular, then plural
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Abend, die Abende\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Nacht, die Nächte\textquotedblright{} — hear the \emph{a} bend to \emph{ä}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Morgen, die Morgen\textquotedblright{} — only the article moved
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which article do German plurals take? (\textbf{die} — always, whatever the gender.) Which of the four day-parts looks the same in the plural? (\emph{Morgen} — \emph{der Morgen, die Morgen}.) What changed in \emph{Nächte} besides the ending? (The vowel — \emph{a} took an umlaut and became \emph{ä}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the German greetings}

\label{lesson:GE-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words — just the day's arc, until the endings are automatic.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hallo} — casual \textquotedblleft{}hi\textquotedblright{} (a \emph{real} cousin of English \textquotedblleft{}hello\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{gut} — \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} \emph{and} \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} ($\leftarrow$ Germanic \emph{*gōdaz} = English \emph{good}; the d$\to$t shift).
  \item \textbf{der / die / das} — \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} and German's \emph{three} genders (kept the neuter).
  \item \textbf{Guten Morgen} $\to$ \textbf{Guten Tag} $\to$ \textbf{Guten Abend} — the daytime arc, all \emph{guten} (masculine nouns).
  \item \textbf{Gute Nacht} — bedtime farewell, \emph{gute} because \emph{Nacht} is feminine.
\end{itemize}

Two threads: \textbf{register} (\emph{hallo} vs \emph{Guten Tag}) and \textbf{agreement} (\emph{guten} for masculine day-parts, \emph{gute} for feminine \emph{Nacht}). And one big idea: German words are \textbf{direct Germanic cousins of English}, reshaped by the High German Consonant Shift (\emph{good$\to$gut}, \emph{day$\to$Tag}, \emph{that$\to$das}).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item greet a friend casually, then politely — \emph{hallo} / \emph{Guten Tag}
  \item the right greeting for right now — morning/day/evening
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Guten Tag\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Gute Nacht\textquotedblright{} — and say why the ending changes
  \item three shift-cousins — gut/good, Tag/day, das/that
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Run Guten Morgen $\to$ Guten Tag $\to$ Guten Abend $\to$ Gute Nacht without hesitating on \emph{guten}/\emph{gute}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which German greeting uses \emph{gute}, not \emph{guten}, and why? (\emph{Gute Nacht} — \emph{Nacht} is feminine.) Next chapter, you will learn to introduce yourself and then build the friendly and respectful ways to address someone.
\end{tcolorbox}
